cases.text: Lynille's pictures are sort of up guards and atom paintings, and Mason's exquisite idols are as national as a jingo poem. Mr. Burkett Foster's landscapes smile at one much in the same way that Mr. Carker used to flash his teeth, and Mr. John Collier gives his sitter a cheerful slap on the back before he says like a shampoo or a Turkish bath. This man, he laments most bitterly the divorce that has been made between decorative art and what we usually call pictures, makes a customary appeal to the last judgment and reminds us that in the great days of art Michelangelo was the furnishing upholsterer. In fact, he is quite severe on Mr. Ruskin for not recognizing that a picture should denote the frailty of man, and remarks with pleasing courtesy in Felicitous Grace that many phases of feeling. Having returned to the royal cavern, Calico first pounded the gong and then sat in the throne, wearing Regato's discarded ruby crown and holding in his hand the scepter which Regato had so often thrown at his head. The cut on his chest is still dripping blood. The ache of his overstrained eyes, even the soaring arena around him with thousands of spectators, retrovialities not worth thinking about. He tells us that at this festive season of the year, with Christmas and roast beef looming before us, similes drawn from eating and its results occur most readily to the mind. I have remained a prisoner only because I wish to be one. And with this, he stepped forward and burst the stout chains as easily as if they had been threads. He asked the handler who was needing his aching muscles.
